tips.title: Practise pronunciation daily
tips.body: Pronunciation is one of the four criteria, so it is 25% of your score. It won't change in a week, but 10 minutes a day for four weeks makes a clear difference. Each day, say one hard sound pair (like vest–west) 20 times and one sentence with correct stress 5 times, out loud.

tips.title: Extend your answers
tips.body: "Yes." "No." "Sometimes." — one-word answers give the examiner nothing to mark. Give at least one reason and one detail in every answer. Practise any Part 1 question in no fewer than 2 and no more than 4 sentences, and record yourself.

tips.title: Master the Part 2 structure
tips.body: Without a structure you run out of things to say in 40 seconds. Follow the card's points in a fixed order — what, when/where, why, feelings — and any topic fills 2 minutes. Practise a cue card with a timer; if you stop before 1:30, do it again.

tips.title: Use advanced vocabulary naturally
tips.body: "Advanced" doesn't mean difficult, it means precise — not "good" but "rewarding", not "very tired" but "exhausted". The word must sound like your own; a big word in the wrong place lowers your Lexical Resource. Listen to a recorded answer, mark every very/good/bad/thing, replace them and say it again.

tips.title: Handle Part 3 abstract questions
tips.body: Part 3 asks about society, the future, causes and effects — not about you. There is no "right" answer; there is opinion + reason + example + the other side. Practise by speaking for 30 seconds from each side on one social topic a day (traffic, online learning, tourism).

tryIt.text: Try it: answer one Part 1 question in 2–4 sentences, then do a timed 2-minute cue card.

tips.title: Fix common grammar mistakes
tips.body: Our mistakes aren't random — the same ten or twelve errors from Bangla grammar keep coming back (I am agree, cousin brother, he/she, since + present). Catch these and your accuracy jumps at once. Read the ten correct sentences aloud once a day until the mistake starts to sound wrong to you.

tips.title: Manage your nervousness
tips.body: Nervousness doesn't take away your English — it takes away your access to it. The cure is preparation and familiarity: know the format, know your first minute, and know what to say when you pause. Do a full 12-minute mock test with a friend as the examiner at least three times; by the third, the fear is halved.

tips.title: Use idiomatic expressions carefully
tips.body: Band 7 asks for "some idiomatic vocabulary" — everyday phrases (be into, get by, once in a blue moon), not proverbs. Use at most one per answer, and only ones you have used many times. Take 3 phrases a week and use each in 3 sentences about your own life.

tips.title: Build fluency through shadowing
tips.body: Shadowing means speaking along with native audio at the same speed, stress and tone. It builds fluency, pronunciation and natural phrasing together — the practice with the biggest return. Take 30 seconds of a podcast or interview: listen once, shadow it 3 times, 10 minutes a day.

tips.title: Prepare topic-specific vocabulary
tips.body: There are hundreds of Speaking topics but only 20–25 categories (work, education, environment, technology, health...). With 10–15 of your own words and collocations ready for each category, words come even for unfamiliar questions. Copy 5 words or phrases from each topic's model answer into your notebook and use them in your own sentences.

tryIt.text: Try it: pick a topic in the library, note 5 useful phrases and use them in your own answers.

tips.title: Fluency is flow, not speed
tips.body: Being fluent doesn't mean speaking fast — rushing blurs your pronunciation and breaks your grammar. A good speaker talks at a natural pace, without stopping or stumbling. Fluency breaks on three things: hesitation, repetition and self-correction.

tips.title: Pause with English phrases, not "umm"
tips.body: Pausing isn't forbidden; native speakers pause too. Silence or "umm/aaa" hurts fluency, but a phrase like "Well,", "Let me think for a second." or "...what's the word..." sounds natural and gives you time to think. Use them like an umbrella — only when needed, about once every 3–4 answers, and vary them.

tips.title: Correct only mistakes that change meaning
tips.body: If a mistake changes your meaning, fix it briefly: "...sorry, I mean I didn't like it." If it's a small grammar slip (article, -s, tense), don't go back — the examiner would hear the mistake plus a hesitation. Keep going.

tips.title: Link your ideas, but don't overuse linkers
tips.body: Linking words turn a list into an argument. In Speaking, conversational forms (I'd say, the thing is, having said that, at the end of the day) sound more natural than Writing forms like Moreover or Furthermore. Use a linker only when you really need to show how two ideas connect; starting every sentence with one is a Band 6 sign.

tips.title: Clarity matters, not accent
tips.body: IELTS doesn't want a British, American or Australian accent — pronunciation measures how easily the listener understands you. Even Band 8 allows a first-language accent if it doesn't block understanding. Work on hard sounds (vest–west, sip–ship), word stress (de-VEL-op, ho-TEL), sentence stress and intonation.

tryIt.text: Try it: practise the hard sound pairs and word stress drills in the pronunciation section.

tips.title: Don't take Part 1 lightly
tips.body: The examiner forms a first impression in the first two minutes, and it's hard to change later. Getting stuck on "What do you do in your free time?" suggests weak basic fluency. A good Part 1 also relaxes you for Part 2.

tips.title: Answer in 2 to 4 sentences
tips.body: One word or one sentence gives the examiner no chance to hear your English. Talking for a minute gets you stopped. Answer + reason + one detail is the right size: "Yes, pretty much every day, actually. I take the bus to work since it's by far the cheapest option."

tips.title: Pick one of three strategies
tips.body: No reason asked (what/where/how long) → Direct Answer + Extension. A like, opinion or hidden "why" → A.R.E (Answer – Reason – Example). Habits or free time → L.D.F (Likes – Frequency – Reason). When in doubt, use A.R.E — it works everywhere.

tips.title: Answer first, and don't echo the question
tips.body: Your first word should be Yes/No/Sort of/It depends — no introduction. Don't just repeat the question's words: "Yes, I'm quite into it, actually" beats "Yes, I like cooking." Never stop at Yes/No; add because, since or the thing is.

tips.title: Add a concrete detail and vary your words
tips.body: "I like music — mostly old Bangla band songs from the nineties" gives the examiner far more language than "I like music". Replace 'very' with quite, pretty, fairly, absolutely or not particularly, and keep present-tense -s correct (she works, it takes). Give the answer that has more to say — truth isn't checked.

tryIt.text: Try it: answer three Part 1 questions using Direct Answer + Extension, A.R.E and L.D.F.

title: Part 2: Notes, Structure and Filling 2 Minutes

tips.title: Write 4 + 1 keywords, not sentences
tips.body: In one minute you can write two sentences at most, and then you'd read them out — reading, not speaking. Writing nothing is also a mistake; nervous, you'll forget the third point. Write one keyword per card line plus one extra sensory detail — five words in capitals, top to bottom.

tips.title: Split your one minute
tips.body: 0–10 seconds: read the whole card and choose one thing, person or event — the first that comes to mind with the most to say. 10–40: write the 4 keywords. 40–50: add the + detail. 50–60: say your first sentence in your head.

tips.title: Follow the five-step talk
tips.body: Opening (~10s): "The skill I've chosen is...". Bullets 1 & 2 (~35s): background in the past tense. Bullet 3 (~35s): how it happened — the story. Explain (~30s): feelings and why it matters, back in the present. Closing (~10s): "So, all in all...".

tips.title: Use lenses to fill 2 minutes
tips.body: If you think you have nothing to say, look through six lenses: time, senses, people, contrast, a moment and meaning. Senses and contrast are your own additions — they turn Band 6 into Band 7. If you run dry, check your note for an unused keyword, switch lens ("Thinking about it now, ..."), or close neatly after 1:20.

tips.title: Avoid the common Part 2 mistakes
tips.body: Don't answer each bullet in one sentence — treat each as 2–4 sentences. Stay personal and specific, not general; memorise the structure, not the content. Keep past stories in past tense, look at the examiner 80% of the time, and give the "explain" line its full 30 seconds.

tryIt.text: Try it: open a cue card, make a 4 + 1 note in one minute, then talk for two minutes.

tips.title: Use A.R.E + Balance
tips.body: Answer with a clear opinion, give a Reason, add an Example, then Balance with the other side: "Having said that..." / "Of course, it depends...". The Balance step shows you can see more than one side and use complex grammar — this is a Band 7 Part 3 answer.

tips.title: Give longer answers than Part 1
tips.body: There is no right answer and no answer key; the opinion you can explain best is the right one. Part 3 answers are 4–6 sentences, 30–45 seconds. Don't stop after two sentences — the examiner will stop you if needed.

tips.title: Hedge your opinions
tips.body: "Governments must ban cars" sounds immature; "I think governments should probably look at restricting cars in city centres" sounds thoughtful. Say "People tend to be less active than they used to be" rather than "People are lazy now". Band 7+ needs this hedging.

tips.title: When you don't know, keep talking
tips.body: Silence is not an option, but all three routes are: guess with a reason ("I'd imagine... because..."), generalise from what you've seen, or narrow the question ("It probably depends a lot on the country. In mine, ..."). You can't stop at "I don't know", but you can say "I don't know, but..." and continue.

tips.title: Avoid the common Part 3 mistakes
tips.body: Talk about people in general ("most families", "in my country"), keeping your own story for the Example step. Use one filler phrase at most, then answer directly. If the examiner challenges you, hold your view: "That's a fair point, but I'd still say...".

tryIt.text: Try it: answer a Part 3 question with A.R.E + Balance in 4–6 sentences.
